проходить.gloss: to go through; to come in

meanings.en: to go through; to come in
meanings.note: Prefix 'про-' indicates movement through, completion, or missing the mark (stem 'ходить'). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to go through; to come in', paired with 'пройти'.

examples.trans: Come in, please.
Come through to the kitchen.

examples.text: Вика, Паша! Как я рад. Проходите, пожалуйста.
examples.trans: Vika, Pasha! I'm so glad. Come in, please.

присаживаться.gloss: to take a seat, to sit down

meanings.en: to take a seat, to sit down
meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'саживаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to take a seat, to sit down', paired with 'присесть'.

related.gloss: not to have a seat (negated infinitive)

examples.trans: Please, have a seat.
He sits down on the edge of the chair.

examples.text: Прошу, присаживайтесь. Позвольте, я сделаю удобнее.
examples.trans: Please, have a seat. Allow me, I'll make it more comfortable.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'so that, in order to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So that there are witnesses.
I'm calling to say thank you.
So that there are witnesses, Samson.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'you', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.
And does the governor support you?

examples.text: Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
There wasn't enough money.

meanings.note: Prefix 'по-' forms perfective verbs or marks a brief/onset action (stem 'ложить'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to put, to lay down', paired with 'класть'.

examples.text: В гроб с собой икру не положишь!
examples.trans: You can't put caviar in your coffin to take with you!
Put the keys on the table.

examples.text: А вот сюда я её и положу! Отличный подарок будет!
examples.trans: Right here is where I will put it! It will be an excellent gift!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'not a (single); neither... nor', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I haven't got a penny.
Not a word!

examples.text: Пятьсот. А у меня ни копейки.
examples.trans: Five hundred. And I haven't got a penny.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'gram' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Это для тебя сто грамм мало!
examples.trans: A hundred grams is a little for you!
Buy two hundred grams of cheese.

examples.text: Мне нужно триста грамм хорошего коньяка.
examples.trans: I need three hundred grams of good cognac.

meanings.note: Common neuter noun meaning 'meat' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Where do you get your meat?
Very tasty meat!

examples.text: И мой тоже готов! А ты где мясо берёшь?
examples.trans: And mine is ready too! Where do you get your meat?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'I', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Chef, I didn't take it.
I don't know.
I'm doing my homework.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'how; as', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How was it in Hungary?
As you all know...
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'time, occasion' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: Just once.
Say it once more.
What do you mean, once?

зайти.gloss: to come in, to drop in

meanings.en: to come in, to drop in
meanings.note: Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to come in, to drop in', paired with 'заходить'.

examples.trans: Come in, please!
I'll drop by in the evening.

examples.text: Ну, как хочешь. Лидия Алексеевна, зайдите, пожалуйста!
examples.trans: Well, as you like. Lidia Alekseyevna, come in, please!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'to, towards', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: There's someone here to see you.
I'm going to Mum's.

examples.text: Аркадий Борисович, извините, тут к вам человек.
examples.trans: Arkady Borisovich, I'm sorry, there's a man here to see you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We could open a salon for you.
This is for you.

examples.text: Для вас можно открыть салон красоты.
examples.trans: We could open a beauty salon for you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That's what you said.
That house is old.
Well, the thing you said.

meanings.note: Prefix 'от-' ('away from, off') marks separation, completion, or response (stem 'ведать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to taste, to sample', paired with 'отведывать'.

examples.text: Мне не терпится отведать твоего соуса.
examples.trans: I cannot wait to taste your sauce.
Taste this pie!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'some, any', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Put on some background noise.
You see, we need some kind of fantastic version.

examples.text: Может, ты забыла про какие-нибудь? — Какие? — Вот эти вот!
examples.trans: Maybe you forgot about some? — Like what? — These right here!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'очный'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('juicy; succulent').

examples.text: Мясо должно стать мягким и сочным.
examples.trans: The meat must become tender and juicy.

examples.text: Но сочные мясные котлеты такие вкусные!
examples.trans: But juicy meat cutlets are so tasty!

examples.text: Мясо получилось очень нежным и сочным.
examples.trans: The meat turned out very tender and juicy.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'very, very much', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town very much.
It's very hard.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'мешной'). Adjective formed with the common Slavic suffix '-н-' from a noun/verb root. Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('funny, ridiculous').

examples.trans: You're so funny!
That's a funny story.

examples.text: Ты такой смешной, Тузик! Кто такой сладкий?
examples.trans: You're so funny, Tuzik! Who's so sweet?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'joke' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: It's a joke.
What kind of jokes are these?
Normal jokes. Where's the money?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'quite, fully, entirely', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: That is quite enough.
That is quite enough for you.

examples.text: Для настоящей любви этого вполне достаточно.
examples.trans: For true love this is quite enough.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ерьёзно'). Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Are you serious?
I mean it.
No way, what, seriously?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'in, into', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: How is it in Hungary?
I grew up in a communal flat.
Hello! How was it in Hungary?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'life' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: That's life.
I want a different life.
Working. Making people's lives better.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I was born and grew up here.
Dad and Mum.

examples.text: Спасибо, спасибо! Как вы все знаете, я родился и вырос в Синеозерске.
examples.trans: Thank you, thank you! As you all know, I was born and grew up in Sineozersk.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian discourse particle adding conversational nuance meaning 'so, then; like that', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: So I shouldn't wait for you?
That's good like that.
So I shouldn't wait for you tonight?

meanings.note: Manner/predicative adverb in '-о', derived from the neuter short form of the corresponding adjective.

examples.trans: Two days isn't enough.
We have little time.

examples.text: Подождите! Два дня — это же очень мало.
examples.trans: Hold on! Two days is far too little.

meanings.note: Abstract feminine noun formed with the Slavic suffix '-ость' ('-ness, -ity') from the corresponding adjective. Common feminine noun meaning 'joy, gladness' in everyday Russian.

examples.text: Он бы сейчас до потолка прыгал от радости.
examples.trans: He would be jumping to the ceiling for joy right now.
What a joy to see you!

examples.text: Мы с радостью сообщаем вам новость. Ваш долг полностью аннулирован!
examples.trans: We gladly inform you of the news. Your debt is completely canceled!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'what', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What's this?
Look what I've got.

examples.text: Привет! Смотри, что у меня есть.
examples.trans: Hi! Look what I've got.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'such, like this', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What is this?
He's so kind.
Pavel Yuryevich, what is this?

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'person; (pl) people' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: He is a good person.
There are a lot of people here.
I know the problems of ordinary people.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'but', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо ещё.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need more.
I want to, but I can't.

examples.text: Мы сделали много, но надо сделать ещё больше.
examples.trans: We've done a lot, but we need to do even more.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'suddenly; all of a sudden', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: Why did it suddenly draw level?
Suddenly it began to rain.

examples.text: Почему он вдруг сравнялся? Мы шли впереди на десять процентов!
examples.trans: Why did it suddenly draw level? We were ten percent ahead!

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'лучаться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to happen, occur'.

examples.text: Но вдруг случается какая-то ерунда, и привычки меняются.
examples.trans: Then suddenly some nonsense happens, and our habits change.

examples.text: На кухне никто не хочет случаться без причины.
examples.trans: In the kitchen nobody wants to happen without a reason.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'some, some kind of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: What nonsense.
Some man called you.

examples.text: Бред какой-то. Но, с другой стороны, чем я рискую?
examples.trans: What nonsense. But on the other hand, what have I got to lose?

meanings.note: Common feminine noun meaning 'nonsense, trifle, nothing' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: That's nothing, I even like it.
Don't talk nonsense.

examples.text: Да ерунда, мне даже нравится. Как тебе твой новый кандидат?
examples.trans: That's nothing, I even like it. How do you like your new candidate?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'вычка'). Common feminine noun meaning 'habit' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: An old Soviet habit.
That is a bad habit.

examples.text: Ангелы мои, это вам! Советская привычка.
examples.trans: My angels, this is for you! An old Soviet habit.

meanings.note: Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to change, alter', paired with 'поменяться'.

examples.trans: People change for the better.
Everything around is changing.

examples.text: Да, люди вокруг меняются к лучшему.
examples.trans: Yes, people around are changing for the better.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'at times, occasionally, sometimes', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся в своей правоте.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize we were right.

examples.text: Порой мы убеждаемся, что были правы.
examples.trans: Sometimes we realize that we were right.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'we', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: We've done a lot.
Our toilet is dirty.

examples.text: Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
examples.trans: Look, how dirty our toilet is!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'thanks to', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And it is all thanks to you.
It is what earns us respect.

examples.text: Но благодаря вам у нас все получилось. Спасибо вам за вас.
examples.trans: But thanks to you, we made it work. Thank you for being you.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian pronominal determiner meaning 'our, ours', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: I love our town.
This is our flat.

examples.text: Я очень люблю наш город. Поэтому я иду на второй срок.
examples.trans: I love our town very much. That's why I'm running for a second term.

meanings.note: Agrees in gender, number, and case with the noun it modifies ('favourite, beloved').

examples.text: А ты готовишь мой любимый торт со сгущёнкой!
examples.trans: And you make my favourite condensed milk cake!
This is my favourite book.

examples.text: А ты готовишь мой любимый торт со сгущёнкой! До вечера, Марина.
examples.trans: And you make my favourite condensed milk cake! See you tonight, Marina.

meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'ейчас').

examples.trans: I'm in the office now.
I'll be right there.

examples.text: Конечно, помогу. Кто у вас сейчас начальник?
examples.trans: Of course I'll help. Who's your boss now?

meanings.note: Prefix 'при-' indicates approaching, attachment, or slight degree of action (stem 'ехать'). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'came', paired with 'приезжать'.

examples.text: Вика, ты на какой машине сегодня приехала?
examples.trans: Vika, which car did you come in today?
Why did you even come here? Empty-handed!

examples.text: Так, успокойтесь все. Сейчас за мной приедут.
examples.trans: Right, everyone calm down. They're coming for me any minute.

соскучиться.gloss: to miss, to grow lonely for

meanings.en: to miss, to grow lonely for
meanings.note: Prefix 'с-' ('together' or 'down from') marks convergence or completion (stem 'оскучиться'). Reflexive/intransitive verb with the postfix '-ся'/'-сь' (historically from the reflexive pronoun 'себя', oneself). Used as an perfective (single completed action) verb meaning 'to miss, to grow lonely for', paired with 'скучать'.

examples.trans: Because I missed you, kitty!
Do you think I didn't miss you?

examples.text: Ты думаешь, я не соскучился? Я уже на стенку лезу!
examples.trans: Do you think I didn't miss you? I'm already climbing the wall!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian clause-linking conjunction meaning 'and, but; so', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: And this is for you.
And where's the toy car?
Dad, did you bring any gum?

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'more; still; yet', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: You've still got some.
You'll be sorry!

examples.text: У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
examples.trans: But you've still got some. Give me just one.

бывать.gloss: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit

meanings.en: to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit
meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to happen, to be (sometimes); to visit', paired with 'быть'.

examples.text: У мужчины бывает не только жена.
examples.trans: A man can have more than just a wife.
That happens.

examples.text: У мужчины, мальчик, бывает не только жена. Это моя девушка.
examples.trans: A man, my boy, can have more than just a wife. She's my girlfriend.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'which, who', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: А что я за мэр такой, который держит своё слово?
examples.trans: And what kind of mayor would I be if I kept my word?

examples.text: Чтобы он вернул деньги, которые украл.
examples.trans: For him to give back the money he stole.

examples.text: Который ему город подарил! И откуда у Аллы Евгеньевны новая шуба!
examples.trans: Which the city donated to him! And where Alla Yevgenyevna got a new fur coat!

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian conversational adverb meaning 'now', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Теперь я начальник нашей стройки. Ты уволен!
examples.trans: Now I'm the boss of our building site. You're fired!

examples.text: Ну что, довольна? Теперь новую работу искать.
examples.trans: Well, happy now? Now I have to look for a new job.
Now I have to look for a new job.

meanings.note: Used as an imperfective (ongoing/repeated action) verb meaning 'to be; there is'.

examples.trans: I have a toy car.
Childhood was hard.
You will be asking for forgiveness.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian personal or demonstrative pronoun meaning 'oneself, myself, himself', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.text: Я и сама хорошо проведу время.
examples.trans: I'll have a good time on my own.

examples.text: Николай Филиппович, простите меня, пожалуйста. Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: Nikolai Filippovich, please forgive me. I don't know myself how it happened.

examples.text: Я сам не знаю, как это произошло.
examples.trans: I don't know myself how it happened.

meanings.note: High-frequency Russian spatial or relational preposition meaning 'for the sake of', inherited from Common Slavic roots and used constantly in natural spoken dialogue.

examples.trans: It's all for us.
I'll do anything for you.
Work, work. It's all for us.

meanings.note: Common masculine noun meaning 'friend' in everyday Russian.

examples.trans: This is Vanya, my childhood friend.

examples.text: Это Паша, мой заместитель. Это Ваня, друг моего детства.
examples.trans: This is Pasha, my deputy. This is Vanya, my childhood friend.
